hook.text: A charge warps the space around it. Another charge placed nearby feels the force.

buildup.text: The electric field is a map of force per unit charge at every point in space.

discovery.text: Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative ones.

twist.text: The field exists even when no test charge is present. Space itself carries the influence.

climax.text: Electric fields accelerate electrons in TV tubes, particle beams, and lightning bolts.

punchline.text: Every charge reshapes the space around it — invisibly.

quiz.question: What do electric field lines represent?
options: The path electrons physically travel through a wire
The direction and strength of force a positive test charge would feel
The magnetic field around a current-carrying conductor

topics.title: Gauss's Law: Flux Through a Surface

hook.text: Wrap an imaginary surface around a charge. The total flux tells you the charge inside.

buildup.text: Electric flux counts how many field lines pierce a surface.

discovery.text: Gauss's law says total flux through a closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by ε₀.

twist.text: The shape of the surface doesn't matter — a sphere, a cube, anything gives the same answer.

climax.text: Engineers use Gauss's law to find fields around wires, plates, and spheres instantly.

punchline.text: Count the flux, know the charge. Gauss made it that simple.

quiz.question: What does Gauss's law relate?
options: Magnetic flux to the current inside a loop
Electric flux through a closed surface to the charge enclosed within it
Voltage across a capacitor to its stored energy

hook.text: Two metal plates facing each other create a uniform electric field between them.

buildup.text: Charge one plate positive and the other negative. The field stores energy.

discovery.text: Capacitance grows with larger plates, smaller gaps, and higher-permittivity dielectrics.

twist.text: The energy isn't in the plates — it's in the electric field between them.

climax.text: Supercapacitors store so much field energy they can start a car engine.

punchline.text: The field between the plates holds the energy — not the metal.

quiz.question: Where is the energy actually stored in a capacitor?
options: In the metal plates themselves
In the electric field between the plates
In the wire connecting the plates to the circuit

hook.text: Slide a sheet of glass between capacitor plates and the capacitance jumps.

buildup.text: Dielectric molecules polarize — their positive ends face one way, negative the other.

discovery.text: This polarization partially cancels the internal field, letting the plates hold more charge.

twist.text: Every dielectric has a breakdown voltage. Push past it and the insulator sparks through.

climax.text: Ceramic, plastic, and tantalum dielectrics let engineers build tiny, high-value capacitors.

punchline.text: An insulator that polarizes stores more charge than air alone.

quiz.question: How does a dielectric increase capacitance?
options: It conducts current between the plates
Its polarized molecules partially cancel the field, allowing more charge storage
It increases the voltage across the plates

hook.text: Sit inside a metal cage during a lightning strike and you won't feel a thing.

buildup.text: A Faraday cage is a conductive enclosure. Charges redistribute on its surface.

discovery.text: The rearranged charges cancel the external field perfectly inside the cage.

twist.text: Your microwave oven is a Faraday cage in reverse — it keeps radiation in, not out.

climax.text: Sensitive electronics, MRI rooms, and military bunkers all use Faraday shielding.

punchline.text: Metal on the outside, silence on the inside. Fields can't get through.

quiz.question: How does a Faraday cage protect its contents?
options: It absorbs all electromagnetic energy and converts it to heat
Surface charges rearrange to cancel the external field inside
Its thick walls physically block electromagnetic waves

topics.title: Electric Potential: Voltage as a Landscape

hook.text: Imagine a hill made of voltage. Charges roll downhill from high potential to low.

buildup.text: Electric potential is energy per unit charge — measured in volts.

discovery.text: Equipotential lines are like contour lines on a map. Charges move perpendicular to them.

twist.text: The field points from high to low potential — always downhill on the voltage landscape.

climax.text: Engineers draw potential maps to design circuit boards and shield against interference.

punchline.text: Voltage is the hill. Current is the ball rolling down it.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between electric field and potential?
options: They are unrelated physical quantities
The field points from high potential to low potential, like downhill on a slope
High potential means weak field; low potential means strong field

topics.title: Magnets: North and South Always Paired

hook.text: Cut a magnet in half and you get two smaller magnets, each with both poles.

buildup.text: Magnetic field lines loop from north pole to south pole outside the magnet.

discovery.text: There are no magnetic monopoles — north and south always come in pairs.

twist.text: Physicists have searched for a magnetic monopole for decades. None found yet.

climax.text: Every magnet, from a fridge magnet to a neutron star, obeys this pairing rule.

punchline.text: Cut a magnet forever — north and south refuse to separate.

quiz.question: What happens when you cut a magnet in half?
options: You get one north piece and one south piece
Each half becomes a complete magnet with both north and south poles
The magnet loses its magnetism entirely

hook.text: In 1820 Oersted noticed a compass needle deflect near a current-carrying wire.

buildup.text: The needle swung perpendicular to the wire. Current creates a circular magnetic field.

discovery.text: The right-hand rule: wrap fingers around the wire in current's direction, thumb points north.

twist.text: This accident linked electricity and magnetism for the first time in history.

climax.text: Every electromagnet, motor, and transformer exists because of this connection.

punchline.text: A twitching compass needle united two forces into one.

quiz.question: What did Oersted's experiment prove?
options: Magnets can generate electric current
Electric current creates a magnetic field around the wire
Compass needles are affected by static electricity

hook.text: Wrap wire around an iron nail and send current through it. Instant magnet.

buildup.text: More turns of wire and more current make the field stronger.

discovery.text: The iron core concentrates the field — it's thousands of times stronger than air.

twist.text: Cut the current and the field vanishes. Permanent magnets can't do that.

climax.text: Scrapyard cranes, MRI machines, and particle accelerators all use electromagnets.

punchline.text: Magnetism you can switch on and off — just add current.

quiz.question: What makes an electromagnet different from a permanent magnet?
options: Electromagnets are always stronger
An electromagnet's field can be turned on and off with current
Permanent magnets use iron but electromagnets don't

topics.title: The Lorentz Force: Charges in Motion

hook.text: A moving charge in a magnetic field gets shoved sideways. Not forward, not backward — sideways.

buildup.text: The force is perpendicular to both the velocity and the field direction.

discovery.text: F = qv × B. The cross product gives the direction. It curves the particle's path.

twist.text: The force does no work — it changes direction but never speed. Kinetic energy stays constant.

climax.text: Cyclotrons, mass spectrometers, and CRT displays all use this sideways force.

punchline.text: The magnetic force is a steering wheel, not an engine.

quiz.question: What direction does the magnetic force act on a moving charge?
options: In the same direction as the charge's motion
Perpendicular to both the velocity and the magnetic field
Directly toward the nearest magnetic pole

topics.title: Ampere's Law: Current and Field Linked

hook.text: Walk a loop around a wire and add up the magnetic field. The total tells you the current inside.

buildup.text: Ampere's law relates the line integral of B around a path to the enclosed current.

discovery.text: For a long straight wire, the field circles the wire and drops as 1/r.

twist.text: Inside a solenoid, the field is uniform. Outside, it's nearly zero — a clean contrast.

climax.text: Ampere's law lets engineers calculate fields in wires, coils, and toroids quickly.

punchline.text: Loop around the wire and the field reveals the current.

quiz.question: What does Ampere's law calculate?
options: The voltage induced in a moving conductor
The magnetic field from the current enclosed by a chosen loop
The force between two parallel charged plates

hook.text: Iron leaps toward a magnet. Aluminum barely reacts. Bismuth actually repels. Why?

buildup.text: Ferromagnetic materials have atomic domains that align and amplify external fields.

discovery.text: Paramagnetic materials align weakly. Diamagnetic materials oppose the field slightly.

twist.text: Heat a ferromagnet past its Curie temperature and it loses magnetism completely.

climax.text: Hard drives store data in tiny ferromagnetic domains — each bit is a magnet.

punchline.text: Iron amplifies. Aluminum yawns. Bismuth pushes back.

quiz.question: What happens to a ferromagnet above its Curie temperature?
options: Its magnetism doubles due to thermal energy
It loses its ferromagnetic properties and becomes paramagnetic
It becomes a permanent magnet that can never be demagnetized

topics.title: Faraday's Law: Changing Fields Make Voltage

hook.text: Move a magnet through a coil and a voltage appears. No battery needed.

buildup.text: A changing magnetic flux through a loop induces an electromotive force (EMF).

discovery.text: The faster the flux changes, the bigger the induced voltage. Speed matters.

twist.text: It works both ways — move the magnet or move the coil. Only relative motion counts.

climax.text: Faraday's law is the foundation of generators, transformers, and wireless charging.

punchline.text: Change the flux and voltage appears from nothing — that's induction.

quiz.question: What does Faraday's law say induces voltage?
options: A steady magnetic field around a conductor
A changing magnetic flux through a loop or coil
Two parallel wires carrying current in opposite directions

hook.text: Push a magnet into a coil and the coil pushes back. Pull it out and it pulls.

buildup.text: The induced current creates its own magnetic field that opposes the change causing it.

discovery.text: This is Lenz's law — induction always works to resist the change in flux.

twist.text: Without Lenz's law, energy would be created from nothing — violating conservation.

climax.text: Magnetic braking on roller coasters uses Lenz's law — eddy currents oppose the motion.

punchline.text: Nature fights every change in flux — that's Lenz's law.

quiz.question: What would happen if Lenz's law didn't exist?
options: Generators would produce more power for free
Energy conservation would be violated — energy could be created from nothing
Magnets would lose their fields permanently

topics.title: Eddy Currents: Loops of Waste and Use

hook.text: Drop a magnet through a copper tube and it falls in slow motion. Eddy currents brake it.

buildup.text: Changing flux induces circular currents in nearby conductors — called eddy currents.

discovery.text: These loops generate their own opposing field, creating drag and heating the metal.

twist.text: Transformer cores are laminated into thin sheets to break eddy current loops and cut losses.

climax.text: Induction cooktops use eddy currents deliberately — the pot heats, the stove stays cool.

punchline.text: Eddy currents are waste in transformers and a feature in cooktops.

quiz.question: Why are transformer cores laminated into thin sheets?
options: To make them lighter and easier to transport
To break eddy current loops and reduce energy losses
To increase the magnetic field strength inside the core

topics.title: Mutual Inductance: Coils Talking to Coils

hook.text: Two coils near each other share magnetic flux. Change current in one and voltage appears in the other.

buildup.text: The shared flux links them. More turns and closer spacing increase the coupling.

discovery.text: Mutual inductance M measures how much voltage one coil gets from current changes in another.

twist.text: Transformers maximize M on purpose. Wireless chargers rely on it too.

climax.text: Unwanted mutual inductance is called crosstalk — it corrupts signals on circuit boards.

punchline.text: Two coils, one changing field — energy transfers without wires.

quiz.question: What causes mutual inductance between two coils?
options: Electrostatic charge buildup between the coils
Changing current in one coil creates flux that links to the other
Physical vibration from one coil transfers to the other

hook.text: A coil fights its own current changes. Speed up the current and it pushes back.

buildup.text: Changing current changes the coil's own flux. That flux induces a back-EMF.

discovery.text: Self-inductance L is measured in henrys. Bigger coils with more turns have higher L.

twist.text: Opening a switch on an inductive load causes a spark — the coil releases stored energy.

climax.text: Inductors in power supplies smooth current. In filters they block high frequencies.

punchline.text: Every coil resists change — that resistance is inductance.

quiz.question: Why does opening a switch on an inductive circuit create a spark?
options: The wire heats up and ignites nearby air
The collapsing magnetic field releases stored energy as a high-voltage spike
Static charge accumulated on the switch contacts discharges

hook.text: Place your phone on a pad and it charges. No plug, no cable, just a magnetic field.

buildup.text: A coil in the pad carries AC current, creating an oscillating magnetic field.

discovery.text: A receiving coil in the phone picks up that field and converts it back to current.

twist.text: Efficiency is about 80% — the rest becomes heat in the coils and air gap.

climax.text: Resonant coupling extends the range — charging through thick cases and at a distance.

punchline.text: No wires needed — just two coils and Faraday's law.

quiz.question: What limits wireless charging efficiency?
options: The phone's battery chemistry rejects wirelessly delivered current
Energy is lost as heat in the coils and the air gap between them
Wireless charging only works with specific radio frequencies

topics.title: Maxwell's First Equation: Gauss for Electricity

hook.text: Maxwell took four equations and unified all of electromagnetism. The first is Gauss's law.

buildup.text: Electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀.

discovery.text: Charges are sources of electric field lines — they start and end on charges.

twist.text: In a region with no charge, field lines can pass through but never originate.

climax.text: This single equation explains Coulomb's law, shielding, and conductor behavior.

punchline.text: Charge is where electric field lines are born and where they die.

quiz.question: What does Maxwell's first equation tell us about electric field lines?
options: They form closed loops with no beginning or end
They originate and terminate on electric charges
They are always parallel to magnetic field lines

hook.text: Electric field lines start on charges. Magnetic field lines never start or end.

buildup.text: The total magnetic flux through any closed surface is always zero.

discovery.text: Every field line that enters a surface must exit somewhere else. No net magnetic charge.

twist.text: If a magnetic monopole were found, this equation would need a new term.

climax.text: Decades of searching have confirmed: magnetic poles always come in pairs.

punchline.text: Magnetic field lines form endless loops — no start, no end.

quiz.question: What does Maxwell's second equation imply?
options: Magnetic monopoles exist but are very rare
Magnetic field lines always form closed loops — no isolated poles exist
Magnetic fields are always stronger than electric fields

topics.title: Maxwell's Third: Faraday's Law in Math

hook.text: A changing magnetic field creates a curling electric field. Maxwell wrote it as an equation.

buildup.text: The curl of E equals the negative time rate of change of B. Compact and complete.

discovery.text: This is Faraday's law in differential form — valid at every point in space.

twist.text: The electric field here isn't caused by charges — it's caused by changing magnetism.

climax.text: This equation predicts how generators, inductors, and antennas work.

punchline.text: Change the magnetic field and an electric field swirls into existence.

quiz.question: What creates the electric field described by Maxwell's third equation?
options: Electric charges distributed in space
A time-varying magnetic field
Steady current flowing through a conductor

hook.text: Ampere's law had a flaw. Maxwell fixed it by adding a missing term.

buildup.text: Current creates a magnetic field. But changing electric fields also create one.

discovery.text: Maxwell added 'displacement current' — a changing E field acts like a hidden current.

twist.text: This fix meant electromagnetic waves could exist — no medium needed, just fields making fields.

climax.text: One extra term predicted radio, light, and all electromagnetic radiation.

punchline.text: Maxwell added one term and discovered that light is a wave.

quiz.question: What was Maxwell's key addition to Ampere's law?
options: He added a term for magnetic monopoles
He added displacement current — changing electric fields create magnetic fields
He replaced current with voltage in the equation

topics.title: Putting It All Together: Four Equations, One Universe

hook.text: Four compact equations describe every electromagnetic phenomenon in the universe.

buildup.text: They link electric and magnetic fields, charges, and currents in a self-consistent framework.

discovery.text: From these four, you can derive Coulomb's law, Faraday's law, and the speed of light.

twist.text: Einstein read Maxwell's equations and realized space and time must be linked.

climax.text: Maxwell's equations are considered the most elegant achievement in classical physics.

punchline.text: Four equations, two fields, one universe. Maxwell saw it all.

quiz.question: How did Maxwell's equations influence Einstein's work?
options: They proved that gravity is an electromagnetic force
They implied a constant speed of light, leading Einstein to develop relativity
They showed that time can only move forward

topics.title: Speed of Light from Two Constants

hook.text: Maxwell calculated the speed of electromagnetic waves and got 300,000 km/s — the speed of light.

buildup.text: He combined two lab-measured constants: ε₀ and μ₀, the permittivity and permeability of space.

discovery.text: c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀). Plug in the numbers and light's speed falls out — no optics needed.

twist.text: This meant light itself is an electromagnetic wave. Optics and electromagnetism merged.

climax.text: One formula from electricity and magnetism explained a mystery that puzzled all of physics.

punchline.text: Two constants of empty space predict the speed of light exactly.

quiz.question: How did Maxwell calculate the speed of light?
options: He measured the time for light to bounce off a mirror
He combined the electric and magnetic constants of space: c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀)
He calculated the frequency times the wavelength of visible light

hook.text: Radio, microwaves, light, and X-rays are all the same thing — just different frequencies.

buildup.text: The spectrum spans from extremely low frequency radio to ultra-high energy gamma rays.

discovery.text: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in vacuum. Only frequency differs.

twist.text: Visible light occupies a tiny sliver — less than 0.0035% of the full spectrum.

climax.text: Humans have harnessed almost every band: radio, Wi-Fi, infrared, UV, X-ray, and beyond.

punchline.text: Light is just the one frequency our eyes happen to detect.

quiz.question: What differentiates radio waves from X-rays?
options: They travel at different speeds in vacuum
They differ only in frequency and wavelength; both are electromagnetic waves
Radio waves are mechanical; X-rays are electromagnetic

hook.text: Push AC into a metal rod and electromagnetic waves fly off into space.

buildup.text: Oscillating current in the antenna creates oscillating electric and magnetic fields.

discovery.text: The fields detach from the antenna and propagate outward at the speed of light.

twist.text: Antenna length matters — a half-wavelength antenna resonates and radiates most efficiently.

climax.text: Every phone, satellite, and radio station depends on antennas tuned to their frequency.

punchline.text: Shake electrons fast enough and they throw light into the void.

quiz.question: Why is antenna length important?
options: Longer antennas receive signals from farther away
A half-wavelength antenna resonates, maximizing radiation efficiency
Shorter antennas produce higher-frequency waves

hook.text: Hertz proved electromagnetic waves exist in 1887 — sparks leapt across a gap in his receiver.

buildup.text: Marconi sent radio signals across the Atlantic in 1901. Wireless was born.

discovery.text: Radio waves bend around hills, bounce off the ionosphere, and pass through walls.

twist.text: AM carries audio by varying wave height. FM varies frequency — clearer but shorter range.

climax.text: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cell signals are all radio waves at different frequencies.

punchline.text: Hertz made sparks. Marconi crossed oceans. Radio changed everything.

quiz.question: How did Hertz prove electromagnetic waves exist?
options: He measured the speed of light with a rotating mirror
He generated sparks that induced detectable signals in a remote receiver
He observed radio waves bending around the Earth's surface

hook.text: A radar engineer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near a magnetron. Microwaves.

buildup.text: Microwaves oscillate water molecules. The friction heats food from the inside.

discovery.text: Microwave ovens use 2.45 GHz — a frequency water absorbs efficiently.

twist.text: Cell towers, Wi-Fi, and satellite links all transmit data on microwave frequencies.

climax.text: 5G networks use millimeter waves — the highest microwave band — for blazing speed.

punchline.text: Microwaves cook your food and carry your data — same physics, different use.

quiz.question: How do microwaves heat food?
options: They heat the air inside the oven, which cooks the food
They oscillate water molecules, generating friction and heat
They emit infrared radiation that penetrates the food surface

hook.text: Fiber optic cables carry the internet as pulses of light — not electrons.

buildup.text: Light bounces inside a glass fiber by total internal reflection. Zero electrical interference.

discovery.text: A single fiber carries terabits per second — millions of phone calls simultaneously.

twist.text: Lasers generate coherent light — all waves in phase. Perfect for fiber communication.

climax.text: Undersea fiber cables carry 99% of intercontinental internet traffic today.

punchline.text: The internet runs on light trapped inside glass threads.

quiz.question: Why are fiber optic cables immune to electrical interference?
options: They are shielded with metal cladding
They carry light pulses, not electrical signals, so electromagnetic noise has no effect
The glass absorbs all external radiation

hook.text: A blender turns on and your radio crackles. Devices leak electromagnetic noise.

buildup.text: EMC ensures devices neither emit too much noise nor break when exposed to it.

discovery.text: Shielding wraps circuits in metal. Filtering blocks unwanted frequencies at ports.

twist.text: Every wire is an antenna. Even a PCB trace can broadcast or receive interference.

climax.text: Medical devices, aircraft, and cars must pass strict EMC testing before sale.

punchline.text: Good engineering means your devices coexist in silence.

quiz.question: What does electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) ensure?
options: Devices run on the same voltage standard worldwide
Devices neither emit harmful noise nor malfunction from external interference
All wireless devices use the same frequency band
